the reason why that original change was wrong, and how it was noticed (ie what the symptoms of the reverted patch were) is important.
So "many small patches" aren't automatically any better than one big one. The thing that matters is to keep things _conceptually_ separated.
The fact is, pointless churn is BAD. It's a real expense.
there can be large and invasive patches that are easy to verify with tooling, so it's not necessarily about the size per se
Without the checking of the result, "build-testing" is just "building", and completely irrelevant.
This is entirely untested, thus the "Not-yet-signed-off-by".
Micro-optimizations need numbers. Otherwise they aren't micro-optimizations, they are just "change code randomly".
but the commit message also has to stand on its own, even _without_ the pointer.
Add the link if it has *ADDITIONAL* information.
This kind of "split up one large patch into many small patches THAT DON'T ACTUALLY WORK INDIVIDUALLY" model is pure and utter garbage.
I repeat: if you cannot explain a merge, then JUST DON'T DO IT.
if you can make an obvious fix in 5 lines, do it.  Don't try to make a clean fix that fixes the problem the clever way in 150 lines.
The code looks fine, but I had to *look* at the code to try to even guess at what the hell you asked me to pull, and that's not fine.
bug reporting and testing is a fundamental part of commit logs, not some secondary thing.

minmax: scsi: fix mis-use of 'clamp()' in sr.c

While working on simplifying the minmax functions, and avoiding
excessive macro expansion, it turns out that the sr.c use of the
'clamp()' macro has the arguments the wrong way around.

The clamp logic is

	val = clamp(in, low, high);

and it returns the input clamped to the low/high limits. But sr.c ddid

	speed = clamp(0, speed, 0xffff / 177);

which clamps the value '0' to the range '[speed, 0xffff / 177]' and ends
up being nonsensical.

Happily, I don't think anybody ever cared.
